pass_a_gloss: [...] from hands the one once taken hold of. For there is not, he says, the one rescuing from my hands. I will do, and who will turn it back? For I have made the calling of the nations, he says, or, I have saved those straying. And who will change this, or remove it toward not being so? For that from the hand of God no one will snatch those saved by him, the Saviour himself will confirm, saying: My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me; and I give them eternal life, and they will surely not perish into the age, and someone will surely not snatch them from my hand. My Father, who has given to me, is greater than all, and no one is able to snatch from the hand of my Father. This is clearly the thing written: There is not the one rescuing from my hands. [Lemma, Isaiah 43:14:] Thus says the Lord God, the one redeeming you, the holy one of Israel: For your sake I will send to Babylon, and I will rouse all those fleeing, and Chaldeans will be bound in ships. Through the things just now said to us having woven no ignoble exhortation for those called from nations into knowledge of him, and having shown that he alone has the knowledge of the things both in beginnings and through the middle and last, and indeed that beside him there is wholly no other who is able to save, and having settled firm faith in them through these things, he moves the words to those from the blood of Israel, and tries to fully assure that he is all-powerful and wonder-working, and that the natures of the things yield to his nods; and the very elements of the world serve, and whatever he himself wills, this wholly is accomplished, nothing lying at the feet [against it]. For it was needed, it was needed, for those from Israel of very much enlightenment, and of the exhortations and reminders that settle them into steadiness of mind, since they slipped aside to the things not lawful, and having inclined to other gods, they sacrificed to idols and to the host of heaven, as it is written; he makes then for them the foretelling of the things to be, and uncovers beforehand the misfortunes of the Babylonians, very skilfully, showing beforehand that they themselves will be captives by those; but proclaiming beforehand that they will suffer the most shameful of all because of them, as I said. And since the word to them was coming about the greatest things, necessarily he shows the incomparable glory of his own power, and indeed the excess of the strength, saying: Thus says the Lord God, the one redeeming you, the holy one of Israel. For so that he might carry them into remembrance of the things of old, of those, I mean, at the redemption that happened from Egypt, when also a great multitude of wonders bore witness to his [the section breaks off].
pass_b_english: … from his hands the one he has once taken hold of. 'For there is no one,' he says, 'who can deliver out of my hands. I will act, and who will turn it back?' (Isaiah 43:13). For I have brought about the calling of the nations, he says, that is, I have saved those who were going astray. And who will change this, or rather alter it so that it is not so?

That no one will snatch from the hand of God those whom he has saved, the Savior himself assures us when he says: 'My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me; and I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand. My Father, who has given them to me, is greater than all, and no one can snatch them out of my Father's hand' (John 10:27–29). This is plainly what is written: 'There is no one who can deliver out of my hands.'
'Thus says the Lord God who redeems you, the Holy One of Israel: For your sake I will send to Babylon, and I will rouse up all who flee, and the Chaldeans will be bound in ships' (Isaiah 43:14).

In the words we have just read he has woven no mean exhortation for those called from the nations to the knowledge of him. He has shown that he alone has knowledge of the things at the beginning, in the middle, and at the end, and indeed that apart from him there is no one at all who can save. Having set faith firmly in them by these words, he now turns his words to those of the blood of Israel, and tries to assure them that he is all-powerful and a worker of wonders, and that the natures of things yield to his nod. The very elements of the world serve him, and whatever he wills is brought to pass without fail, with nothing standing in its way.

For it was necessary, truly necessary, that those of Israel should have the fullest enlightenment, and the exhortations and reminders that would settle them in firmness of mind, since they had slipped into what is unlawful, and, inclining to other gods, had sacrificed to idols and to the host of heaven, as it is written (compare Acts 7:41–42; Jeremiah 19:13). So he foretells to them what will be, and very skillfully reveals beforehand the misfortunes of the Babylonians. He shows in advance that they themselves will be taken captive by the Babylonians, but he also proclaims in advance, as I said, that the Babylonians will suffer the most shameful things of all because of them.

Since the word addressed to them concerned the greatest matters, he must show the incomparable glory of his power and the surpassing greatness of his strength, saying: 'Thus says the Lord God who redeems you, the Holy One of Israel' (Isaiah 43:14). choices.english: will suffer the most shameful things of all
choices.why: πείσονται is from πάσχω, 'they will suffer', not from πείθω; the Babylonians suffer because of Israel.

choices.english: with nothing standing in its way
choices.why: Nothing lies in the path of what God wills.
Keeps the weaving image for the exhortation.
παναλκής, of all strength; God's power over the elements.
Cyril glosses 'I will act' as the calling and salvation of the Gentiles.
